name: Power dissipation
seoDesc: Power dissipation: work out resistor 10 (R₁₀) from the resistor 1 and the resistor 2. A free physics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Give the Power dissipation calculator the resistor 1, the resistor 2, the resistor 3 and the resistor 4 and it returns resistor 10 (R₁₀). Think of it as a shortcut for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Power dissipation calculator work?
sections.html:
The Power dissipation calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports resistor 10 (R₁₀) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the connection type); then you type in the resistor 1 (R₁), the resistor 2 (R₂), the resistor 3 (R₃) and the resistor 4 (R₄).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Power dissipation calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Resistor 10 (R₁₀)=-resistor 1 (R₁) − resistor 2 (R₂) − resistor 3 (R₃) − resistor 4 (R₄) − resistor 5 (R₅) − resistor 6 (R₆) − resistor 7 (R₇) − resistor 8 (R₈) − resistor 9 (R₉) + rs
Resistor 10 (R₁₀)=resistor 1 (R₁) × resistor 2 (R₂) × resistor 3 (R₃) × resistor 4 (R₄) × resistor 5 (R₅) × resistor 6 (R₆) × resistor 7 (R₇) × resistor 8 (R₈) × resistor 9 (R₉) × rp ÷ (resistor 1 (R₁) × resistor 2 (R₂) × resistor 3 (R₃) × resistor 4 (R₄) × resistor 5 (R₅) × resistor 6 (R₆) × resistor 7 (R₇) × resistor 8 (R₈) × resistor 9 (R₉) − resistor 1 (R₁) × resistor 2 (R₂) × resistor 3 (R₃) × resistor 4 (R₄) × resistor 5 (R₅) × resistor 6 (R₆) × resistor 7 (R₇) × resistor 8 (R₈) × rp − resistor 1 (R₁) × resistor 2 (R₂) × resistor 3 (R₃) × resistor 4 (R₄) × resistor 5 (R₅) × resistor 6 (R₆) × resistor 7 (R₇) × resistor 9 (R₉) × rp − resistor 1 (R₁) × resistor 2 (R₂) × resistor 3 (R₃) × resistor 4 (R₄) × resistor 5 (R₅) × resistor 6 (R₆) × resistor 8 (R₈) × resistor 9 (R₉) × rp − resistor 1 (R₁) × resistor 2 (R₂) × resistor 3 (R₃) × resistor 4 (R₄) × resistor 5 (R₅) × resistor 7 (R₇) × resistor 8 (R₈) × resistor 9 (R₉) × rp − resistor 1 (R₁) × resistor 2 (R₂) × resistor 3 (R₃) × resistor 4 (R₄) × resistor 6 (R₆) × resistor 7 (R₇) × resistor 8 (R₈) × resistor 9 (R₉) × rp − resistor 1 (R₁) × resistor 2 (R₂) × resistor 3 (R₃) × resistor 5 (R₅) × resistor 6 (R₆) × resistor 7 (R₇) × resistor 8 (R₈) × resistor 9 (R₉) × rp − resistor 1 (R₁) × resistor 2 (R₂) × resistor 4 (R₄) × resistor 5 (R₅) × resistor 6 (R₆) × resistor 7 (R₇) × resistor 8 (R₈) × resistor 9 (R₉) × rp − resistor 1 (R₁) × resistor 3 (R₃) × resistor 4 (R₄) × resistor 5 (R₅) × resistor 6 (R₆) × resistor 7 (R₇) × resistor 8 (R₈) × resistor 9 (R₉) × rp − resistor 2 (R₂) × resistor 3 (R₃) × resistor 4 (R₄) × resistor 5 (R₅) × resistor 6 (R₆) × resistor 7 (R₇) × resistor 8 (R₈) × resistor 9 (R₉) × rp)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.html:
Take Connection type set to Series, Power = 10 and Rs = 10. The calculator returns Voltage = 10 V.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Voltage, opening in volts
  • Resistance – ohms, opening in ohms

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Power dissipation calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the resistor 1, the resistor 2 and the resistor 3 — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Power dissipation calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns resistor 10 (R₁₀), derived from the resistor 1, the resistor 2 and the resistor 3. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Power dissipation calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the resistor 1, the resistor 2, the resistor 3 and the resistor 4, which is 12 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter voltage in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Voltage opens in volts and the chip beside it offers 6 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Voltage = 10 V. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Power dissipation calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
